title: The five in authority
hook: decisions are made through five chosen Sikhs

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jathedar: leader of a band, and the head of a Takht who serves it. Your line was the leader of the takht.

Drums first, then flags. A street has been cleared for a nagar kirtan, a Sikh procession: families in their best clothes, a float carrying the Guru Granth Sahib under a canopy. And walking out front, ahead of everything, five Sikhs dressed alike, swords held upright. Those five lead. Count back through this block and the number keeps turning up: five who give amrit, five who hear a confession and set a tankhah. It isn't decoration. In the Sikh way of doing things, when something weighty must be decided, it goes to five.
screen: `FIVE WALK AHEAD OF THE PROCESSION.` → `FIVE AT AMRIT, FIVE AT TANKHAH.` → `WEIGHTY THINGS GO TO FIVE.`

segments.voice: Begin where the number begins: the panj pyare, the five beloved ones at Anandpur. In the tradition's telling, the Tenth Guru not only initiated them but asked to be initiated by them, and at Chamkaur, as this path told long ago, the five ordered the Guru to leave the fort, and he obeyed. So from the start, five chosen Sikhs could speak with an authority the Guru himself honored. The Sikh Rehat Maryada carries that into ordinary life: when amrit is given, five give it; when a breach is confessed, five decide the tankhah. Three things about how it works. First, the five are chosen for the task, from among Sikhs who keep the code. The authority belongs to the role, not the person's rank; a shopkeeper can stand beside a scholar. Second, five is enough that no single will can rule the room, and few enough to actually sit together and decide. One person can be swayed by a grudge, a crowd by a mood. Five have to talk. Third, the pattern scales up. At the Akal Takht, the heads of the Takhts and senior granthis can sit together as five, the Panj Singh Sahiban, to decide matters for the whole panth. A village sangat and the throne of the Timeless use the same shape. Behind it is the conviction this block keeps returning to: the Guru is present where the Khalsa gathers.
screen: `AT CHAMKAUR, THE GURU OBEYED THE FIVE.` · `FIVE GIVE AMRIT, FIVE SET TANKHAH.` · `CHOSEN FOR THE TASK, NOT BY RANK.` · `THE SAME SHAPE AT THE AKAL TAKHT.` · then, large: `FIVE DECIDE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small decision you've been carrying alone, and picture four people you trust sitting around it with you, not to vote it away from you but to talk. Hear each of them ask you one question, and notice which question you'd rather not answer; stay with that one.
The five in authority. In Sikh practice, weighty decisions go to five chosen Sikhs, from the amrit ceremony to the Akal Takht. Today's word.
Your line: five decide. One person can be swayed; five have to sit and talk. Back tomorrow.

chat.says: Why do Sikhs keep putting big decisions to five people instead of one leader?
options: It goes back to the panj pyare; five can't be ruled by one will, yet can still decide.
Five is simply a lucky number in Punjab, so it's used to bring good fortune.
The five hold their seats for life, so their rank alone gives them the final say.
chat.meaning: The pattern begins with the panj pyare. Five chosen for the task are enough that no single will rules, and few enough to decide.
